items.title: L5: Choosing between vacancies and managing deadlines
items.source: Civil Service Jobs website; GOV.UK, Working for the Civil Service
items.body: When two or more vacancies interest you, decide using the facts in the adverts. Compare the closing dates first, because an application cannot be made after the closing time and a job that closes soon may need to come first. Compare the essential criteria and ask which role you can evidence best, since a strong match is worth more than a higher salary you may not reach. Compare the location, working pattern and journey time, because a job you cannot reach or fit around your commitments will not work. Compare the assessment methods: a role that uses a personal statement needs writing time, while one with timed tests needs practice. Check the security level, because higher levels take longer and have residence rules. Note the grade, which shows the level of responsibility. For a first Civil Service job, Administrative Officer is a common starting point. Keep a record of each vacancy with its reference number, closing date and stage. Applying to several roles is normal and sensible, but quality matters more than quantity, so give each the time it needs. If two closing dates fall together, finish the stronger match first, and submit it a few days early. If a technical problem stops you submitting, contact the department using the contact in the advert at once and explain. Do not assume that late applications will be accepted. Keep screenshots or emails showing any fault.

questions.prompt: Lena has two vacancies she likes. One closes tomorrow, the other in ten days. Both suit her equally. What is the best plan?

options.text: Write the later one first, as it will be the stronger application
Write the later one first, since it will be the stronger application of the two
Finish and submit the one that closes tomorrow, then work on the other
Apply for the later one only, since it gives more time to prepare

questions.hint: Deadlines decide the order when fit is equal.

questions.prompt: Which factor should usually outweigh a slightly higher salary when choosing between two vacancies?

options.text: How many other people are likely to apply for each of the vacancies
How new the department's website looks
How long the advert is
How well you can evidence the essential criteria

questions.hint: A strong match gives a better chance.

options.text: Skipping the advert to save time

items.title: L5: Profile and account problems
items.body: Account problems are common and usually fixable if you act early. If you cannot log in, use the password reset option on the site. A reset link goes to the email address on your account. If you no longer have access to that email address, contact the support route given on the Civil Service Jobs website. Do not make a new account, because duplicate accounts can cause confusion about your applications. If your phone number or email has changed, update your profile straight away so invitations reach you. If you applied but cannot see the application, check you completed all stages and that you were not left in a draft. Draft applications are not submitted. A submitted application normally produces a confirmation, so keep it. If messages are missing, check junk or spam folders and make sure your mailbox is not full. Add the sender address to your safe senders list if your email service allows. Use a trusted device and a secure connection rather than public wifi when you log in. Never share your password and never give it to anyone who contacts you, even if they say they work for the Civil Service. If you think your account has been misused, change your password and report it. Treat any email asking for bank details or a fee as suspicious. When in doubt, go directly to the website by typing its address rather than following a link in a message.

options.text: Phone every department to ask for help
Use the password reset option on the site

items.title: L5: Spotting errors in application answers
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Assessors score what is written against the criteria, so common errors cost marks. The first error is a vague claim, such as I am a good communicator, with no example. The second is the wrong focus: an answer about a time you led a team when the question was about helping a colleague. The third is describing what the group did, using we, so the assessor cannot tell what you did. The fourth is leaving out the result, so the answer ends without showing that the action worked. The fifth is writing a long account of the situation and only one line about the action. The sixth is exceeding the word limit, since text beyond it may not be read. The seventh is leaving out something the question asked for, such as two examples. The eighth is careless spelling, which is a poor sign for accuracy in administrative roles. The ninth is an invented or exaggerated example, which can be exposed at interview or in the checks. To avoid these, read each question twice and underline the key words. Plan the answer using STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Spend most words on the Action. Say I. Give numbers where you can. Check word counts. Read the answer aloud. Compare it with the criterion and ask whether an assessor could score it from what is written.

questions.prompt: Which answer to a question about helping a colleague has the wrong focus?

options.text: A story about helping a new starter learn a computer system step by step
A story of covering for a colleague who was ill
An account of a time the writer led a large project
A story of explaining a process to a team mate

questions.hint: The answer must match the question.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with the sentence We cleared the backlog and the manager was pleased?

options.text: It names the manager
It uses numbers
It is too long and includes the manager, who should not be mentioned

options.text: I sorted the post each morning, and complaints about late post fell to none that month
I sorted the post each morning, saving the team about an hour a day
I sorted the post each morning, and my manager asked me to train a new starter
I sorted the post each morning and passed urgent items to my manager

options.text: Add more detail about the situation so the assessor sees the context

options.text: It changes the closing date

questions.hint: Every part of the question counts.

options.text: Make the claim longer and stronger so it sounds more convincing

items.title: L5: Test day situations
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Test day goes best with preparation, but problems can still arise. If your invitation gives a window of days, choose a time when you will not be disturbed, and do not leave it to the last day, because a fault then may leave no time to rerun. Before you start, check your device, internet and any equipment named in the invitation. If you are disabled or have a health condition and have not asked for reasonable adjustments, contact the department before you begin, not afterwards. During the test, keep an eye on the clock, answer the easy questions first if the test allows going back, and guess rather than leave blanks if there is no penalty. In a verbal test, answer only from the passage. In a numerical test, check units. In a situational judgement test, pick the response consistent with the Civil Service Code. If something goes wrong, such as the connection drops or the screen freezes, do not repeat the test on your own. Note the time and what happened, take a screenshot if you can, and contact the number or email on the invitation immediately. Be honest about the fault. Do not ask another person to sit the test for you or help you, since tests may be rechecked later. After the test, you may be told the result by email. If you did not do as well as you hoped, ask for feedback and practise for next time.

questions.prompt: Imran has a seven-day test window. When should he take the test?

options.text: At the busiest time of day, to be sure the website is working
On the final evening, when he expects to have most time
Early in the window, in a quiet slot, leaving time for a rerun
Whenever the invitation email is next opened on his phone

questions.hint: Early leaves room to deal with problems.

questions.prompt: Zara has dyslexia and has not asked for adjustments. The test starts in an hour. What should she do?

options.text: Ask a friend to sit the test on her behalf

options.text: Note the time, take a screenshot and contact the invitation's contact

questions.prompt: Why is it a mistake to repeat a test on your own after a fault?

options.text: It is not what the rules allow and it can look like cheating

questions.prompt: Ben finds the first five questions hard and the clock is running. If the test allows going back, what is sensible?

options.text: Spend all the time available on the first hard question until solved

options.text: True

options.text: Leaving it alone because it was not your task

Pointing out the mistake to the colleague who made it

The test will be marked more gently

items.title: L5: Interview situations
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Interviews rarely go exactly to plan, so it helps to know how to respond. Panels of two or three people ask the same questions of every candidate and score each answer against the criteria. Prepare two or three real examples for each behaviour listed in the advert, written in STAR form. If a question asks about a time you dealt with a difficult customer and you have no workplace example, use another setting such as volunteering, family life or a shop. If your mind goes blank, say Could I take a moment to think? and pause. If you realise that your chosen example does not fit, say so and move to a better one. If a question is unclear, ask for it to be repeated. If the technology fails, stay calm, rejoin and use the number in the invitation. For strengths questions, answer quickly and honestly, since the panel is looking for energy and natural responses, not rehearsed lines. Say I rather than we. If asked about a mistake, describe a real one, say what you did to put it right and what you learned. Do not blame others. At the end, when asked if you have questions, ask something about the team or the work. Do not ask about pay or holidays first. Afterwards, note what you would change and wait for the outcome. If you are unsuccessful, ask for feedback.

questions.prompt: A panel asks Nia about a difficult customer and she has never had a customer-facing job. What can she do?

options.text: Use an example from volunteering, family life or a shop
Describe a workplace she has never been in

Describe something she watched on television

options.text: Stare at the screen until the panel moves on

options.text: Stay calm, rejoin and use the number in the invitation

options.text: By repeating wording from the advert

items.title: L5: Sift and outcome situations
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: The way a department handles outcomes follows patterns that are useful to know. After the closing date, applications are sifted against the criteria. If you pass, you are invited to the next stage. If you do not, you are usually told by email and can ask for feedback. When many people reach the standard, the department may raise the pass mark so that the numbers fit the places available, so a good answer may still be sifted out. After interviews, the best-scoring candidates who meet the standard are offered the posts. Others who reached the standard may be placed on a reserve list for a set period. A conditional offer is made subject to checks. Candidates sometimes face a situation where outcomes overlap. If you are offered one job while another application is still going, you can tell the second department that you have an offer and ask when they expect to decide. They may or may not be able to speed up. If you accept the first and later get the second, you can withdraw from the first, but it is better to decide early and be polite. A department may withdraw an offer if the checks are not cleared or if information was false. If you are not told the result after the stated time, send a polite query using the contact in the advert.

questions.prompt: Tariq passes a sift but a friend with a similar answer does not. What may explain this?

options.text: The assessors scored only the first sentence

questions.hint: Pass marks can fall between similar scores.

items.title: L5: Pre-employment check situations
items.source: Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Checks raise practical problems, and a few principles solve most of them. Honesty comes first. If you cannot remember an exact date, check old payslips, emails or tax records and give your best accurate estimate, marked as such. If you had a gap, such as caring for a child, being unwell or being unemployed, say so and give someone who can confirm it, such as a family member or a benefit or tax record. If a referee has left their company, ask the company for a replacement contact. If you have no recent employer, a personal referee, such as a teacher or a volunteer manager, may be accepted, depending on the department's rules. For identity, original documents are needed. If your name has changed through marriage or deed poll, provide the certificate. If your passport has expired or is lost, tell the department and ask which other documents are accepted. For right to work, UK nationals usually show a passport or other listed documents; others may use an online share code. If you have a conviction that is unspent, declare it. The department will consider it and rules on spent convictions apply. Respond to requests quickly, since delay can push back your start date. If a check takes longer than expected, ask for an update politely. Keep copies of everything. Do not resign or sign a lease on the strength of a conditional offer.

questions.prompt: Kim cannot remember the exact month she left a job two years ago. What should she do?

options.text: Check old payslips or emails and give her best accurate date
Invent a different job for that period

Choose a neat date that looks tidy

items.title: L5: Security clearance and eligibility situations
items.source: Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK; National Security Vetting
items.body: Eligibility and clearance rules produce real decisions. The advert's eligibility statement says who can apply, and rules depend on your own status. Many jobs are open to UK nationals and to citizens of some other countries and people with certain immigration permissions. Some jobs, especially those involving national security, are reserved for UK nationals. If you are unsure whether you are eligible, use the contact in the advert before you spend time on the application. Clearance levels beyond BPSS include Counter Terrorist Check, Security Check and Developed Vetting. Many entry-level roles need only BPSS. Higher levels can take months and often have minimum residence periods. Vetting asks about your finances, past addresses and associates. Concealment is worse than a difficulty that you declare. Debts or past problems do not automatically stop clearance. The question is whether they create a risk, such as being open to pressure, so honesty and managing debts help. If an advert needs a level of clearance you cannot yet get, such as a residence rule you do not meet, it is not for you right now, but other vacancies may be. If you already hold clearance from earlier work, tell the department, since it may be transferable if it is still valid. Keep your address history ready, because vetting forms ask for past addresses over a number of years.

questions.prompt: Faith is a citizen of another country with permission to work in the UK. How should she find out whether she can apply?

options.text: Assume the answer is yes and apply, as nationality is rarely checked

Ask a friend in a different department

questions.prompt: Why might a national security job be reserved for UK nationals?

options.text: It is only for a short time
It involves very sensitive information

items.title: L5: Fairness situations and complaints
items.source: Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles; Equality Act 2010
items.body: Applying the Recruitment Principles to real cases helps you spot what is fair. Appointments are on merit after fair and open competition. A panel member who scores a friend higher than the evidence supports breaches merit. A department that asks one candidate more difficult questions than others, without reason, breaches fairness. An advert that is only shared with some people breaches openness. A rule such as must be under 30 is likely to be age discrimination. A requirement for a specific qualification may be lawful if it is genuinely needed for the job. A department giving a disabled candidate extra time is making a reasonable adjustment, which is lawful and fair. If you think you were treated unfairly, first gather facts: dates, names and what was said. Raise the issue with the department using its complaints process, and ask for feedback. If you remain dissatisfied, you can bring a complaint to the Civil Service Commission about whether the Recruitment Principles were breached. The Commission looks at process, not whether you should have got the job. For discrimination, there are other routes, such as ACAS early conciliation and the employment tribunal, which have strict time limits, so seek advice early. Complaining does not count against you in later applications. Departments should handle complaints seriously and fairly.

items.title: L5: Disability Confident and adjustment situations
items.source: Disability Confident scheme, GOV.UK; Equality Act 2010
items.body: Real cases show how the guaranteed interview and reasonable adjustments work. A disabled applicant who meets the minimum criteria for the role is offered an interview if they opt in. Meeting the minimum criteria means meeting the essential requirements. The guaranteed interview does not guarantee the job, and the interview is scored in the same way as everyone else's. Reasonable adjustments are changes to remove disadvantages. In a test they could be extra time, a different format, a screen reader or rest breaks. At interview they could be questions in advance, a sign language interpreter, a step-free venue, or a break. At work they could be a specialist keyboard, a quiet desk, flexible hours or time off for appointments. Ask for adjustments through the contact in the advert and as early as possible. You do not need a formal diagnosis, but you should say what the effect is and what would help. The department decides what is reasonable, weighing practicality, cost and the effect on you, and it must consider the request properly. Asking does not count against you. If an adjustment is not working, ask for a change. Information you give about disability is treated in confidence and used to make arrangements. If you are unsure whether a condition counts as a disability, you can still ask the department, and you may find that it does under the Equality Act 2010.

items.title: L5: Flexible working and caring situations
items.source: GOV.UK, Flexible working; Civil Service Jobs adverts
items.body: Many people apply for Civil Service jobs while caring for children or relatives, so practical planning matters. Check the working pattern in the advert before applying. If it says part-time, job-share or flexible working is considered, you can apply for that pattern. If it is silent, ask the contact. Term-time working, compressed hours and flexitime may be possible in some roles. Public-facing jobs may need set hours. Interviews and tests may take place during the working day, so arrange childcare or cover in advance and tell the department if you need a different time, since they may be able to offer one. A video interview from home needs a quiet room and a plan for interruptions. When you receive an offer, check that the pattern you were promised is in your contract or statement of terms. Part-time pay, pension and leave are normally proportionate to hours. Employees have a legal right to request flexible working from day one, and the employer must consider the request reasonably, but may refuse for specific business reasons. A good request is specific about the days and hours and how work will be covered. Look at the effect on benefits or tax credits if you receive them, and seek advice if unsure. Gaps in work history due to caring are fine if explained honestly. Describe the skills you gained, such as organising, budgeting and communicating.

items.title: L5: Scam and safety situations
items.source: Civil Service Jobs website; GOV.UK; Action Fraud guidance
items.body: Recruitment scams copy the look of real adverts and messages. Knowing how genuine recruitment works helps you decide quickly. Genuine Civil Service recruitment is free. It does not ask you to pay to apply, be tested, be trained or be given equipment. Genuine adverts appear on the Civil Service Jobs website with a department, grade, closing date and contact. Genuine interviews follow an application. Messages that offer a job with no application, promise high pay for little work, use a free email address or a messaging app for an interview, or press you to act quickly are warning signs. Genuine identity checks happen after a conditional offer through the department's official channels, not by sending photos of documents to a stranger on a messaging app. Never give your password, bank details or National Insurance number in reply to an unexpected message. If you are unsure, do not click links. Go to the website directly and check your account, or use the contact in the genuine advert. If you paid or shared details, contact your bank at once, change passwords and report to Action Fraud. Tell the department as well. Keep screenshots. Scams can happen to anyone, so reporting quickly protects you and others.

items.title: L5: Putting it all together: a case study from advert to start date
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Disability Confident guidance
items.body: Consider a person, Chris, who has been caring for a relative for four years and has no formal qualifications. Chris finds an Administrative Officer vacancy using a saved search with alerts. The advert says the closing date is in ten days, the pattern is full time with flexible working considered, the essential criteria include accuracy and clear communication, and the assessment is a sift on two behaviours, an online test and a video interview. Chris has a health condition and opts in to the guaranteed interview commitment and asks the contact for extra time in the test. Chris plans backwards, drafts answers using STAR from caring and volunteering, and submits three days early. A sift result arrives by email inviting Chris to the test. Chris practises, takes the test in a quiet room within the window, and passes. The video interview is on a stated date. Chris tests the camera the day before and answers with real examples, using I. A few days later Chris receives a conditional offer. The offer asks for identity documents, referees and an explanation of the caring years, with a person who can confirm them. Chris replies quickly. After some weeks the checks clear and a start date is confirmed in writing. Only then does Chris tell the current part-time employer. On the first day Chris meets the line manager and starts induction. Along the way Chris kept a record of the reference, closing date and stage.
